newsitem.title: UK: NatWest Markets hampered in quest for boss.
newsitem.headline: NatWest Markets hampered in quest for boss.

text.p: NatWest's quest to replace former investment banking chief Martin Owen will be hampered by question marks hanging over its strategy, bankers said on Thursday.
"It's difficult when the guy being considered doesn't know if he is going to have the rug pulled from under his feet. It makes it very difficult to hire somebody," one City headhunter told Reuters.

Owen left NatWest Markets, the investment banking arm of Britain's National Westminster Bank Plc, last month in the wake of the discovery of a multi-million pound "black hole" in the firm's derivatives division.
The 90 million pound ($152 million) loss -- run up over a two-year period -- has also led to the resignations of five senior staff and a major rethink of NatWest Markets' strategy.
NatWest managed to cut the loss to 77 million pounds by clawing back staff bonuses and setting it against provisions it had already made.

But the overhaul, under the leadership of NatWest Group chief executive Derek Wanless who has also taken on the role of head of the Markets division until Owen's successor is appointed, is one of the main factors making it so tough to select the right person.
The idea is to improve controls and risk management as well as speeding up the production of acceptable returns in key business areas.
NatWest said it would focus on areas where it has a competitive advantage and deploy capital in areas where it thinks better returns can be achieved.

Wanless said this would mean shifting away from areas such as the large corporate loan market -- where banks lend huge sums at increasingly tight margins -- to areas such as wealth management which generate regular fee income without being capital intensive.
NatWest is keen to stress the process is a business review rather than the withdrawal from investment banking some have portrayed it as.

But the bank, and Wanless, have been under intense pressure from institutional investors to improve returns, with the costs associated with the relatively risky world of investment banking seen as a drain.

And recent merger rumours involving NatWest and a host of names in the world of financial services, including Barclays Plc and Prudential Corp, have fuelled the uncertainty for both those inside and outside the organisation.

A redefinition of NatWest's strategy in investment banking could become known when it announces its half-year results next month. But if a chief executive has not been appointed by then it will mean the firm has been without a full-time head for nearly two months.
"Until they decide as an organisation what the line is going to be, it will be quite hard to get anyone from the outside," one banker said.
Banking sources said the search for Owen's replacement would have to start within the organisation but ultimately it was likely to be an outside appointment.
"I suspect they will bring someone in from outside," the headhunter said, although he was not aware that an executive search firm had been called in to find the right candidate.
There has been no shortage of suggestions for a new head, althouh three weeks after Owen left, the search for a replacement continues.
NatWest was unwilling to say when a successor would be appointed or when the reshaping of the NatWest Markets business would be completed.

"We are in the process of trying to identify a suitable candidate. Clearly we want to ensure we find the right person to undertake this important role and once we have done that we will be making an announcement," a spokesman told Reuters.
The firm is keeping an open mind on whether the appointment would be internal or from the outside.

Another key element in attracting the right person to take on the difficult role will be the terms of the package on offer. This will become public knowledge when NatWest produces its report and accounts, assuming he or she is a director of the parent bank.
In 1996 Owen was the highest paid director and the director owning most shares in the NatWest group. His total package was 815,000 pounds for the year, including his bonus and pension.

Although Owen handed back 200,000 of his 500,000 pound bonus after the options losses emerged, at the end of 1996 he had shares worth 700,000 pounds at today's price and unexercised options over a further 167,000 shares.
But if NatWest is to compete with rival BZW, the investment banking arm of Barclays, it will have to pay the market rate. And BZW found chief executives do not come cheap.

Bill Harrison, who BZW poached from independent merchant bank Robert Fleming as last September, received a total of 2.852 million pounds for his efforts to the end of the year. This included a golden handshake of 1.5 million pounds in cash. ($ = 0.593 British Pounds)
